notes: Application (firmware) catalog. Every app declares the transports it supports and the wiring recipe for each transport; board pins are referenced by role (@uartTx, @v5, @usbDp, ...) so new boards only need pin roles, not new wiring code.

apps.name: Wi-Fi Print Server (Arsin Print Server)
apps.tagline: Make any printer wireless over Wi-Fi with a full web dashboard.
apps.summary: The flagship build: turns a serial, parallel or USB printer into a network printer. Serves a complete web app (designer, maintenance, configuration) from the board itself, exposes a raw TCP 9100 print port, advertises itself with mDNS as arsin_print_server.local and reconnects to your office Wi-Fi forever.
features: Full responsive web app served from the device (Persian/English, RTL aware)
Label designer with text, barcodes (8 symbologies), QR, images, shapes and variables
Raw TCP 9100 + IPP-ish HTTP print endpoint, so POS apps and CUPS can drive it
mDNS: http://arsin_print_server.local - no IP hunting
Stores up to 5 Wi-Fi networks and always reconnects to the last working one
Maintenance console: self test, status query, calibration, head/nozzle check, counter reset
OTA firmware update and configuration backup/restore from the browser
Job queue with history, byte counters, error log and webhooks
requirements: Board with Wi-Fi (every supported ESP32/ESP8266/Raspberry Pi model)
5V power supply with at least 1A for the board + printer logic
Correct logic level between board and printer (3.3V vs 5V TTL)
A printer that accepts raw data (ESC/POS, ZPL, TSPL, EPL, CPCL, ESC/P or plain text)

transports.name: UART / COM port (TTL)
transports.description: Solder or plug onto the printer mainboard TTL serial port - the most universal option.

transports.name: USB host (printer USB cable)
transports.description: Board acts as USB host; the printer keeps its own USB cable. Needs USB OTG hardware.

transports.name: Parallel / Centronics (DB25)
transports.description: Legacy parallel port printers (dot matrix, old inkjets) driven over GPIO with level shifters.

serial.title: TTL serial wiring (board UART -> printer serial port)
serial.summary: Four wires plus a ground reference. Cross TX and RX, never connect the printer 5V rail to the board.
serial.power: Power the board from its own 5V supply and the printer from its original adapter.

links.printer: Printer RX (DB25 pin 3 / RJ45 pin 6 / header RX)
links.note: Board transmit -> printer receive. If your printer is 5V TTL add a 1k/2k divider or a level shifter.

links.printer: Printer TX (DB25 pin 2 / RJ45 pin 4 / header TX)
links.note: Needed for status queries, calibration replies and job completion detection.
Always connect ground first; a missing ground is the most common cause of garbage output.
Optional hardware flow control - lets the bridge wait when the printer buffer is full.

cables.note: Use a different colour for TX, RX and GND
Across the board 5V and GND rails if the printer shares the supply
Only if the printer port is 5V TTL

steps: Power everything off and unplug the printer.
Identify the printer serial port: DB25 pin 2 (TX), pin 3 (RX), pin 7 (GND) or the RJ45/header equivalent.
Connect board GND to printer GND.
Connect board TX (see pin list) to printer RX through the level shifter if the printer is 5V TTL.
Connect printer TX to board RX.
Set the printer DIP switches to the fastest supported baud rate (115200 recommended) with 8N1 and hardware flow control off.
Power on, open http://arsin_print_server.local, pick the printer language and press Test print.
prerequisites: Soldering iron or a JST/Dupont crimp tool
Multimeter to confirm 5V/3.3V and GND before connecting
Printer service manual or a pinout photo of its serial port
warnings: Never connect the printer 24V/5V rail to a board GPIO.
Some printers use RS-232 levels (+/-12V) on the DB25 port - those need a MAX232 style adapter, not a direct TTL connection.

usbhost.title: USB host wiring (printer USB cable -> board USB port)
usbhost.summary: No soldering to the printer: the board enumerates the printer as a USB device and forwards print data.
usbhost.power: Use a powered USB hub or a 5V/2A supply - USB printers can pull 500 mA plus motor peaks.

links.note: On ESP32-S3/S2 the 5V pin supplies the USB bus; on Raspberry Pi the port supplies it.

cables.item: USB-A to USB-B (or USB-C) printer cable

cables.note: Only for Raspberry Pi Zero / micro-USB boards

steps: Plug the printer USB cable into the board USB host port (native USB port on ESP32-S3/S2, any port on Raspberry Pi).
Power the board from a separate 5V supply or a powered hub.
Open the web app, go to Configuration > Connection, choose 'USB host' and press Detect printer.
The bridge reports the USB VID/PID, manufacturer and product string, then installs the right language profile.
Press Test print to confirm.
prerequisites: A board with USB OTG host support (ESP32-S3, ESP32-S2, Raspberry Pi) - ESP8266 and ESP32-C3 cannot do this
USB printer cable that fits both ends
warnings: USB printers that require a proprietary driver (most inkjets and lasers) only work through the Raspberry Pi build with CUPS.
Do not power a laser printer from the board 5V rail.

parallel.title: Parallel / Centronics wiring (GPIO -> DB25)
parallel.summary: Legacy parallel printers are driven as a raw byte stream: 8 data lines, STROBE, BUSY and GND.
parallel.power: Printer has its own mains supply; the board only drives logic lines.

links.note: Use a 74HCT245 buffer powered from the printer 5V rail.
Flow control: never pulse STROBE while BUSY is high.

steps: Wire the 8 data lines through the buffer, then STROBE, then BUSY and ground.
Select 'Parallel' as the transport in the web app and set the strobe delay (1-10 us).
Send the ESC/P self test page to verify every line.
prerequisites: GPIO bit-banging build (Raspberry Pi or ESP32 with the parallel build)
warnings: Parallel ports are 5V TTL: always buffer the ESP32 3.3V GPIO with a 74HCT245.

apps.name: Bluetooth Print Server (SPP)
apps.tagline: Pair the printer like a headset - Bluetooth Classic SPP, no network needed.
apps.summary: Turns a serial/USB printer into a Bluetooth SPP device that Android POS apps, Windows Bluetooth printers and phones can pair with. Includes the same web app, served over Wi-Fi when configured, and a Bluetooth pairing PIN screen.
features: Bluetooth SPP (serial port profile) with configurable device name and PIN
Auto-reconnect to the last paired host
Wi-Fi fallback: the same web app is reachable when Wi-Fi is configured
Raw byte passthrough so any app that prints to a Bluetooth printer works
Live link statistics: bytes in/out, disconnects, latency
requirements: ESP32 (original) or Raspberry Pi - the ESP32-S3/S2/C3/C6 and ESP8266 have no Bluetooth Classic
Printer serial or USB connection as described in the wiring section
5V 1A supply

transports.name: UART / COM port (TTL)
transports.description: Printer connected over TTL serial; the Bluetooth link replaces the cable to the till or phone.

transports.name: USB host + Bluetooth
transports.description: USB printer plus Bluetooth SPP output (Raspberry Pi or ESP32-S3 with BLE fallback).

serial.title: Bluetooth SPP bridge wiring (no host cable)
serial.summary: Only the printer side is wired; the host (till, tablet, phone) connects over Bluetooth.
serial.power: Board on 5V USB, printer on its own adapter.

links.note: Used to read printer status back over the Bluetooth link.

cables.item: Antenna clearance: keep the board 1 cm away from metal and the printer PSU
cables.note: Bluetooth range suffers badly inside a metal chassis

steps: Wire TX/RX/GND to the printer serial port.
Flash the Bluetooth build and open the web app (Wi-Fi AP arsin_print_server if no Wi-Fi is configured).
Set the Bluetooth device name (default arsin_print_server) and PIN (default 0000).
Pair from the phone/till, then select the printer in the POS app.
Print a test receipt to confirm the raw passthrough works.
prerequisites: A POS app or OS that supports Bluetooth SPP printing
warnings: Bluetooth Classic throughput is ~100 kB/s: fine for receipts, slow for large raster labels.
Some iOS apps only support AirPrint/IPP - use the Wi-Fi or Raspberry Pi build for those.

usbhost.title: USB printer + Bluetooth output
usbhost.summary: The printer plugs into the board over USB; the till talks Bluetooth.
usbhost.power: Use a powered hub when the printer draws more than 500 mA.
steps: Plug the printer into the board USB host port.
Choose USB host as the transport in the web app.
Pair over Bluetooth and print a test page.
prerequisites: Board with USB OTG host support
warnings: USB printers that need a proprietary driver are not supported by this build.

apps.name: Bluetooth LE Print Server
apps.tagline: Modern BLE bridge for ESP32-C3/C6/S3 and phones.
apps.summary: Exposes the printer over a Bluetooth Low Energy GATT service (Nordic UART style TX/RX characteristics plus a battery/status service) so mobile apps and modern POS terminals can print without a network.

requires.excludeReason: The BLE build is ~1.99 MB, which does not fit the 1.875 MB application slot of the largest OTA partition scheme on a 4 MB ESP32. Use the ESP32-S3/C3/C6 builds for BLE (as this app is intended), or the Bluetooth SPP build on the classic ESP32.

features: BLE GATT UART service (6E400001-B5A3-F393-E0A9-E50E24DCCA9E) with TX/RX characteristics
Device Information service with model, firmware version and serial number
Configurable advertising name and connection parameters (latency/power tuning)
Works on ESP32-S3/C3/C6 which have no Bluetooth Classic
requirements: Any BLE capable board
Printer serial or USB connection
Client app with BLE GATT write support

transports.name: UART / COM port (TTL)
transports.description: Printer on TTL serial, BLE on the air.

serial.title: BLE bridge wiring
serial.summary: Identical to the Bluetooth SPP wiring - only the printer side is connected.
serial.power: Board 5V USB, printer on its own supply.
steps: Wire TX/RX/GND to the printer.
Flash the BLE build and set the advertising name in the web app.
Connect from the client app to the GATT UART service and write print data to RX.
Check the live byte counter in the web dashboard.
prerequisites: Client app that supports GATT writes
warnings: BLE MTU limits each write to 20-512 bytes - the firmware reassembles the stream automatically.

usbhost.title: USB printer + BLE output
usbhost.summary: USB printer into the board, BLE to the client.
steps: Plug the printer into the board.
Select USB host in the web app.
Connect over BLE and print.
prerequisites: Board with USB OTG host support

apps.name: USB Host Print Server
apps.tagline: Plug the printer into the board - Wi-Fi and USB host in one build.
apps.summary: Dedicated USB host build: the board enumerates the printer, exposes it on TCP 9100 and the web app, and can also serve the printer to Bluetooth hosts. Ideal for modern USB thermal printers that have no serial port.
features: USB printer enumeration with VID/PID detection and automatic language profile
Bulk endpoint streaming with flow control and 4 kB buffering
USB printer reset and port cycling from the web app (fixes stuck jobs)
Full web app, TCP 9100 and mDNS as in the Wi-Fi build
requirements: Board with USB OTG host (ESP32-S3/S2, Raspberry Pi)
5V 2A supply or powered hub
USB printer cable

transports.name: USB host (printer USB cable)
transports.description: The printer keeps its own cable; no soldering to the printer board.

usbhost.title: USB host wiring
usbhost.summary: One USB cable between the printer and the board - no printer disassembly.
usbhost.power: Powered hub or 5V/2A supply; laser printers must never be powered from the board.

cables.note: Keeps the board rail stable during thermal print peaks

steps: Connect the printer USB cable to the board native USB port.
Power the board and watch the web app Device page: the printer appears with its VID/PID.
Choose the language profile (auto-detected from the USB descriptor where possible).
Print a self test page, then add the printer to the POS app as a network printer on port 9100.
warnings: Some USB printers present a proprietary interface instead of the standard printer class; those need the Raspberry Pi + CUPS build.
Keep the USB cable shorter than 1.5 m for reliable enumeration.

apps.name: Serial / COM Port Bridge
apps.tagline: Raw serial to TCP: the universal COM-port-to-network adapter.
apps.summary: A transparent bidirectional serial bridge: anything you send to TCP 9100 or the web console goes out of the printer port byte for byte, and printer replies are streamed back. Perfect for diagnosing a printer, driving it from legacy software, or writing your own protocol.
features: Transparent TCP <-> UART bridge with configurable baud, data bits, parity and stop bits
Web serial console with hex/text send, timestamps and receive buffer download
Line-ending and delay injection for old firmware that needs pacing
Byte counters and CRC error detection on the serial line
requirements: Any supported board
3.3V/5V level matching
Printer serial pinout

transports.name: UART / COM port (TTL)
transports.description: Direct TTL serial connection to the printer.

transports.name: USB-serial adapter (COM port passthrough)
transports.description: Use a USB-serial adapter as the printer port (Raspberry Pi: /dev/ttyUSB0).

serial.title: Serial bridge wiring
serial.summary: Three wires (TX, RX, GND) plus optional flow control.
serial.power: Board and printer each on their own supply; only GND is shared.

links.note: Enable hardware flow control for large print jobs.

cables.note: Handy for first-time baud rate discovery

steps: Wire TX, RX and GND between the board and the printer.
Open the web serial console and set the baud rate (try 9600, 19200, 38400, 115200).
Send 1B 40 (ESC @) as hex and look for the printer initialising.
Save the profile and connect legacy software to port 9100.
warnings: Do not connect RS-232 (+/-12V) directly to the board.

usb-bridge.title: USB-serial adapter as the printer port
usb-bridge.summary: A USB-serial cable is the printer link; the board still bridges it to the network.
usb-bridge.power: The adapter is powered from the board USB port.
steps: Plug the adapter into the board USB port.
Select the adapter in the web app port list (/dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux).
Match the baud rate and open the serial console.

apps.name: Hybrid Print Server (Wi-Fi + Bluetooth + USB host)
apps.tagline: Every transport in one build - enterprise ready.
apps.summary: The all-in-one build for ESP32-S3 class boards and Raspberry Pi: Wi-Fi web app, TCP 9100, mDNS, Bluetooth SPP/BLE, USB host printer support and serial fallback, with the full maintenance console and label designer.
features: All transports at once: Wi-Fi, TCP 9100, mDNS, BLE, USB host and serial fallback
Automatic transport failover: if Wi-Fi drops, BLE and the serial port keep working
Enterprise extras: API keys, webhooks, job history, remote reboot, OTA, config backup
Full label designer and maintenance console served from the device
requirements: ESP32-S3 / ESP32-S2 / Raspberry Pi (needs Wi-Fi + USB host)
5V 2A supply
USB printer cable or TTL serial wires

transports.name: USB host (printer USB cable)
transports.description: USB printer plus Wi-Fi, BLE and serial fallback.

transports.name: UART / COM port (TTL)
transports.description: Serial printer with Wi-Fi + BLE front ends.

usbhost.title: Hybrid USB host wiring
usbhost.summary: USB printer cable plus (optionally) the serial fallback wires.

links.note: Optional: keeps printing if the USB link fails.

steps: Connect the USB printer cable to the board.
Optionally wire the serial fallback pair.
In the web app enable the transports you want and set the failover order.
Create an API key for the POS system and add the printer as network printer port 9100.
warnings: Running Wi-Fi, USB host and BLE at once peaks around 900 mA - use a 2A supply.

serial.title: Hybrid serial wiring
serial.summary: TTL serial printer with Wi-Fi, BLE and USB-serial fallback available.
serial.power: Board 5V 2A, printer on its own adapter.
steps: Wire TX/RX/GND.
Set the baud rate and language in the web app.
Enable Wi-Fi and BLE in the transports panel.

apps.name: Raspberry Pi CUPS Bridge
apps.tagline: Full Linux print server: vendor drivers, AirPrint, IPP Everywhere.
apps.summary: Installs the Arsin print server plus CUPS on Raspberry Pi OS, so printers that need a real driver (inkjets, lasers, GDI-only units) become network and AirPrint printers. The Arsin web app drives CUPS, adds the label designer, nozzle/head maintenance and the job history.
features: CUPS with IPP Everywhere, AirPrint and Samba (Windows) sharing out of the box
Vendor .ppd driver support for inkjets and lasers
Arsin web app on top: label designer, maintenance console, job history, users and API keys
Automatic printer detection (USB, network, serial) with a guided driver picker
Ink/toner level reading where the driver exposes it, plus nozzle check and cleaning routines
requirements: Raspberry Pi (Zero 2 W and up recommended) with Raspberry Pi OS Lite
microSD card 8 GB or larger
5V 2A (Zero) / 5V 3A (Pi 4/5) power supply
Printer with USB or network interface

transports.name: USB host (printer USB cable)
transports.description: Plug the printer into the Pi and CUPS does the rest.

transports.name: Network printer (Ethernet / Wi-Fi)
transports.description: The printer is already on the network; the bridge adds the designer, maintenance console and job history.

transports.name: Serial / USB-serial adapter
transports.description: TTL serial or a USB-serial adapter on /dev/ttyUSB0.

usbhost.title: Raspberry Pi USB printer wiring
usbhost.summary: No wiring at all beyond the printer USB cable - the Pi supplies the port.
usbhost.power: Pi on its own 5V supply; the printer keeps its mains adapter.

links.note: The Pi USB port provides up to 1.2 A total across all ports on Pi 4/5.

cables.note: For laser printers or several devices

steps: Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite to the microSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager and set the Wi-Fi, hostname and SSH in the advanced options.
Boot the Pi, connect over SSH and run the one-line installer (see the install page).
Open http://arsin_print_server.local and follow the first-run wizard.
Add the printer: the wizard lists USB printers and suggests drivers (including raw for ESC/POS/ZPL units).
Enable AirPrint/IPP sharing if phones and tablets should print directly.
prerequisites: SSH or a monitor+keyboard for the first boot
warnings: GDI/winprinters (very cheap lasers with no PPD) still cannot work - use a raw ESC/POS/ZPL printer for those.
Keep the Pi on a UPS or clean power: a brown-out during a print job can wedge the USB bus.

network.title: Network printer + Pi bridge
network.summary: The Pi talks to the printer over the LAN; no direct wiring.
network.power: Pi on 5V, printer on its own supply.

links.note: Only needed for wired printers; Wi-Fi printers just need the IP address.

steps: Give the printer a static IP (or DHCP reservation).
Enter that IP in the Arsin wizard as a socket:// printer.
Optionally enable AirPrint sharing from the Pi.

serial.title: Raspberry Pi serial wiring (40-pin header)
serial.power: Pi on 5V; printer on its own adapter; share only GND.

links.note: Enable the serial port in raspi-config (login shell disabled, hardware enabled).

cables.item: Dupont jumper wires (female-female for the 40-pin header)

steps: Run sudo raspi-config > Interface Options > Serial Port: login shell off, hardware on.
Wire pin 8 (GPIO14 TX) to printer RX, pin 10 (GPIO15 RX) to printer TX and pin 6 to GND.
Select /dev/serial0 in the Arsin wizard and set the baud rate.
Send the self test from the maintenance page.
